socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize announced a new 2026 ARC-AGI-2 Kaggle high of 88.06% by Tufa Labs and said a $150,000 bonus would be split among teams scoring above 85%.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A public-board threshold announcement and major standings lead; the post does not establish a final private score.

socialPosts.author: masspeakss
socialPosts.summary: masspeaks reacted in Japanese to Tufa Labs exceeding 85% on ARC-AGI-2, calling the result impressive. The public board independently shows Tufa Labs at 88.06% in the afternoon snapshot.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Respectful reaction from a current ARC-AGI-2 mover to the leader.

socialPosts.author: masspeakss
socialPosts.summary: In a Japanese post, masspeaks said careful preparation had paid off and expected a high gold-band cutoff. This is the contestant’s reaction; the post alone does not establish the exact score or method.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Context from the ARC-AGI-2 public-board mover; compare any score or rank with the board brief.

socialPosts.author: tufalabs
socialPosts.summary: In a reply to Mike Knoop’s ARC-AGI-2 bonus-threshold post, Tufa Labs said it had not set out to solve ARC-AGI-2, started by accident, and plans to share more after the deadline. This is the team’s account, not an independently established history.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: First-person context from the ARC-AGI-2 public-board leader; no method or final result is disclosed.

socialPosts.author: JFPuget
socialPosts.summary: Puget asked ARC Prize whether the 85% bonus threshold refers to the public or private leaderboard; no organizer answer was visible in the checked thread.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Flags a reporting question; avoid presenting the public score as the final prize result.

socialPosts.author: mikeknoop
socialPosts.summary: Knoop said ARC-AGI-2 remains much harder than ARC-AGI-1 and that eventual open solutions will be useful to study, while quoting his earlier reaction to Tufa Labs crossing the public Kaggle bonus threshold.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Organizer context about the contest; his forward-looking statement is not a released solution or final award.

socialPosts.author: mikeknoop
socialPosts.summary: Knoop said the 85% Grand Prize bonus threshold had been reached on Kaggle and called 2026 the final ARC-AGI-2 Kaggle year.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Provides organizer context for the Tufa Labs result; his expectation about future open artifacts is not yet a release.

socialPosts.author: fchollet
socialPosts.summary: Chollet reacted to ARC Prize’s Tufa Labs ARC-2 announcement by saying Kaggle scores are getting very good.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A founder reaction adds a measured voice to the organizer’s score announcement.

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize announced Stephen Wolfram as a keynote speaker for its 2026 Research Summit.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A current event-program lead for the meeting digest.

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize published verified Grok 4.7 scores: 1.8% on ARC-AGI-3 with its standard harness, 10.0% with a provider adapter, and 61.4% on ARC-AGI-2.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: The harness distinction matters when comparing model scores; the post reports organizer verification.

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize published verified DeepSeek V4.1 Flash scores of 72.9% on ARC-AGI-2 and 94.5% on ARC-AGI-1, with stated per-task costs.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A dated organizer model verification relevant to ARC-2 comparisons.

socialPosts.author: fchollet
socialPosts.summary: Replying to Michael Taiwo’s suggestion of a small-budget version students could run before attempting the full experiment, Chollet called it a great idea. The conversation concerns his previously announced KerasHub/JAX/TPU post-training experiments; it does not announce a release, schedule or ARC score.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A modest follow-up to the archived post-training lead: student accessibility is a possible direction welcomed by Chollet, not a promised deliverable or evidence of a competition method.

competitorFacts.text: ARC Prize named Tufa Labs and its Duck agent the first-place open-source solution for the June 2026 ARC-AGI-3 Milestone 1 prize.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Tufa Labs — Duck Harness technical overview
competitorFacts.text: Tufa Labs says its public Duck harness lets an LLM inspect game grids as image and text, write Python in a REPL, and keep context short by evicting older messages. This describes the published Milestone 1 system, not an unverified current submission.
Tufa Labs lists Dries Smit, Isaiah Pressman and Jeroen Cottaar among its AI researchers, with research interests spanning reinforcement learning, self-play and Bayesian methods.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Tufa Labs — October 9 public competition post
competitorFacts.text: On October 9, 2026, Tufa Labs described a temporary setback in a public X post and said it remained dedicated to crushing competitors with overwhelming resources and compute.
Yi-Chia Chen’s Kaggle profile lists her as a Competitions Master and a double-degree student at National Taiwan University and Waseda University.

The 2025 NVARC team write-up credits sorokin and cpmpml. Both handles appear in the observed roster of the distinct 2026 NVARC3 entry. This does not establish an affiliation for every current member.

NVIDIA describes the separate 2025 NVARC ARC-AGI-2 solution as using synthetic data generation, test-time training and a fine-tuned 4B model. This is historical background, not a claim about the 2026 NVARC3 agent.

The rostered lukasaichberger Kaggle profile identifies its owner as Lukas Aichberger and links to his research website.
Johannes Kepler University Linz lists Lukas Aichberger at its Institute for Machine Learning and credits him on research about reasoning models and uncertainty evaluation.
Another rostered account, fses91, describes itself on Kaggle only as Florian; the public profile does not establish a surname.
The rostered dwellement0baser Kaggle profile identifies its owner as Mykyta Ielanskyi.

Johannes Kepler University Linz lists Mykyta Ielanskyi at its Institute for Machine Learning. Its research record credits him and Lukas Aichberger together on a 2026 paper about reward redistribution for reasoning models.
The ARChitects’ own 2025 solution write-up credits David Hartmann under the Kaggle handle dvhrtm, alongside Jan Disselhoff (insanitycheck) and Daniel Franzen (dfranzen).
The team’s 2025 technical report lists David Hartmann at Lambda, Inc.
The sole rostered michaeltgao Kaggle account displays the public name Michael; the profile does not establish a surname.
The Kaggle account and team both use the public name Lord Han Solo. The profile itself does not supply a verified personal name.

socialPosts.author: OCEANVIN10
socialPosts.summary: OCEAN highlighted the Memento 3 preprint. Its authors report that a fixed language model revises an external rulebook and executable world model; on the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, they report clearing every level with fewer actions than the human baseline. These are author-reported results on the public set.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A new ARC-AGI-3 research lead for the edition desk. The paper provides a concrete mechanism and results, but the public tutorial set cannot establish private-game performance.

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize announced Yi-Chia Chen at 59.17% on the 2026 ARC-AGI-3 Kaggle board, taking the lead over Tufa Labs.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A new public-board leader is the strongest ARC-3 standings lead; verify the current board before an edition.

socialPosts.author: crysis44k
socialPosts.summary: Posting in Japanese, fshindo said the ARC-AGI-3 competition had taught them a great deal about agent harnesses and called contests a valuable learning opportunity. The post links the current Kaggle competition.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A fresh first-person account of the engineering lessons behind the competition. The author handle is observed directly; no team or real-person identity has been established.

socialPosts.author: mikeknoop
socialPosts.summary: Mike Knoop said the same thing is happening with ARC-AGI-3 while quoting Pedro Domingos’s comment that models are absorbing harness behavior. The quoted post links Harness Learning Enables Generalizable Test-Time Adaptation. Knoop gives no named team, method, score or ARC experiment. The linked paper trains a proposer to revise executable harness code using feedback; its reported evaluations cover reasoning and multi-hop question answering, so the ARC-3 observation remains Knoop’s attributed comment.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Fresh ARC co-founder reaction for reporting on how models and harnesses divide the work. Useful research context, with no new verified Kaggle result or evidence that harnesses disappear.

socialPosts.author: Fei2411
socialPosts.summary: FeiZ reported a one-level ls20 ARC-AGI-3 comparison: a DS Bot cleared that level within 81 steps, while a DeepSeek Harness exhausted 110 steps without clearing it. This is the author’s own small test, not a Kaggle standing or verified benchmark result.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Recent ARC-AGI-3 community experiment; the author explicitly says one level proves little.

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize announced Stephen Wolfram as a keynote speaker for its 2026 Research Summit.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A current event-program lead for the meeting digest.

socialPosts.author: SimonOuellette6
socialPosts.summary: Ouellette released an ARC-AGI-3-style training-data framework with 429 playable games, solvers and demonstration generators; he said 37 games still lacked solvers. The linked repository says it combines augmented public ARC demos and other game sources.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A concrete research resource; its author describes training material, not a measured Kaggle-score gain or coverage of private games.

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize published verified Grok 4.7 scores: 1.8% on ARC-AGI-3 with its standard harness, 10.0% with a provider adapter, and 61.4% on ARC-AGI-2.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: The harness distinction matters when comparing model scores; the post reports organizer verification.

socialPosts.author: GregKamradt
socialPosts.summary: Kamradt invited researchers to contact ARC Prize about red-teaming future ARC-AGI benchmarks and mentioned grants and credits as possible support.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A direct research-participation lead; it is an invitation, not a claim about any current contestant’s approach.

socialPosts.author: fchollet
socialPosts.summary: Replying to Michael Taiwo’s suggestion of a small-budget version students could run before attempting the full experiment, Chollet called it a great idea. The conversation concerns his previously announced KerasHub/JAX/TPU post-training experiments; it does not announce a release, schedule or ARC score.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: A modest follow-up to the archived post-training lead: student accessibility is a possible direction welcomed by Chollet, not a promised deliverable or evidence of a competition method.

socialPosts.author: pmddomingos
socialPosts.summary: Pedro Domingos described a linked paper as showing the model absorbing the harness. The primary release, submitted September 28, describes learning to revise executable harnesses from execution feedback, with reasoning and multi-hop question-answering evaluations. Its introduction retains an executable harness and frozen models at test time. The social phrasing is Domingos’s interpretation; it should not be reported as a demonstrated removal of the harness or an ARC competition result.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Primary quoted context for Mike Knoop’s new ARC-AGI-3 reaction. Group by the shared paper and distinguish its actual experiment from the broader social interpretation.
